question: A 30-year-old metal worker presents with a foreign body sensation after grinding work. The vision is reduced and there is a small dark spot on the cornea with surrounding chemosis. The MOST appropriate immediate action is:

answers.text: Irrigate the eye copiously with normal saline and attempt manual FB removal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Irrigation and manual pressure techniques are absolutely contraindicated when a penetrating FB is suspected — they risk expulsing intraocular contents.

answers.text: Refer immediately to an ophthalmologist without applying pressure or patching tightly; shield the eye

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A dark corneal spot + reduced vision after high-velocity metal work = penetrating (intraocular) FB until proven otherwise. Apply a protective shield (NOT a pressure pad), and refer urgently. Pressure of any kind risks catastrophic prolapse of uveal contents.

answers.text: Apply topical anaesthetic and remove the foreign body with a cotton bud

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cotton bud removal applies surface pressure and is appropriate only for superficial conjunctival FBs — never when a penetrating FB is suspected.

answers.text: Prescribe topical antibiotics and ask the patient to return in 24 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Deferring assessment by 24 hours is dangerous here. A penetrating metallic IOFB can cause siderosis bulbi, endophthalmitis, and permanent vision loss within hours to days.

overallFeedback.feedback: Key safety rule: any suspicion of penetrating FB is a contraindication to ocular pressure, irrigation, or manipulation at primary care level. Use an eye shield (not a pad) and refer urgently. Reduced vision + dark corneal spot after metal grinding = IOFB until proven otherwise.
Correct. The critical rule: high-velocity metal FB + reduced vision = open globe until proven otherwise. Shield the eye (no pressure patch), and refer urgently for X-ray/CT and surgical exploration.
